extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, IPC classifiers, patent attorneys, and patent searchers
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and interpretive guidance for assigning International Patent Classification (IPC) places to patent document subject matter, including definitions of scope, expressions, categories of subject matter, and special rules for chemical matter, groups, subgroups, and residual places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions clarify the exact boundaries of the subject matter appropriate for a classification place and provide supplementary information to classification entries but do not change their scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions are prepared following a structured format; the definition statement gives a detailed explanation of the scope using relevant words/phrases (sometimes alternative to title wording) found in patent documents. Definitions may also explain limiting/informative references, interpret special classifying rules affecting the place, and define terms used. Definitions are provided only for a limited number of subclasses and groups and will be elaborated further where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-limiting References
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting references indicate locations of subject matter that could be of interest for searching but do not limit the scope of the associated classification places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduced progressively into Definitions to facilitate patent searches; they are informative only and do not change classification scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical Structural Formulae and Graphic Illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical structural formulae and other graphic illustrations are used in chemistry-related IPC areas to define or interpret the scope of classification places and to illustrate content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulae are introduced in the scheme of the Classification when necessary for defining scope; many additional formulae are introduced in Definitions as examples. Formulae and graphics are available through hyperlinks in classification entries. Other explanatory graphics may be used similarly in Definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'Covered' or 'Provided for'
rubrics_metrics.description: When subject matter is stated to be 'covered' by/in a classification place, it means the subject matter has characteristics enabling it to be classified in that place; 'provided for' has the same meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are cited (e.g., group A41F 18/00) to show usage; treat the two expressions as equivalent for classification purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions Indicating Residual Subject Matter ('not otherwise provided for')
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions such as 'not otherwise provided for' mean 'not provided for in any other group in the same subclass or in any other subclass' and designate residual subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to group, class, or subclass titles. Groups worded '... not provided for in groups ...' cover subject matter not provided for in the stated groups. 'Other...' groups cover matter not provided for in related groups at the same hierarchical level. Residual main groups (often 99/00) are usually located at the end of subclasses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions Indicating Combination Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups that designate subject matter 'covered by more than one of main groups...' provide for subject matter consisting of combinations of characteristics not covered as a whole by a single specified group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such group wording may also provide for subject matter not covered by any of the groups in a specified range; both combination-of-characteristics cases and 'not covered by any' cases are possible (example: C05B 21/00).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'i.e.' and 'e.g.'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'i.e.' has the sense of 'equals' and indicates equivalence/definition; 'e.g.' gives one or more examples and does not limit the preceding wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'i.e.' means the two phrases should be considered equivalent. 'e.g.' is used to provide a typical illustration, to draw attention that what follows is included in the preceding wording even if not apparent, or to indicate matter covered by a group for which no dependent subgroup exists (multiple examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Connectives: 'A and B', 'A or B', 'Either A or B, but not Both'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A and B' requires presence of both in the same example/ embodiment; 'A or B' implies presence of A or B or both; 'either A or B, but not both' implies presence of A or B but not both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret these connectives literally when reading group/subgroup titles and examples; apply to presence/combination of characteristics in embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'In general', 'Per se', 'Specially adapted for'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In general' indicates characteristics considered irrespective of specific application; 'per se' concerns only the item itself as opposed to a combination; 'specially adapted for' indicates things modified or particularly constructed for a given use or purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples to decide classification (e.g., 'Content per se' vs content generation in distribution). Titles or groupings with these phrases should be interpreted according to these senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'Or the like'
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'or the like' emphasises that a classification place is not limited to the specific examples mentioned and also covers similar subject matter with essentially the same characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such wording as inclusive of similar items (example provided: 'Non-abrasive sharpening devices for scythes, sickles, or the like').

rubrics_metrics.name: Glossary Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-part Glossary is included: the first part covers classification terms and expressions relating to principles and rules; the second part covers technical terms and expressions used in the Classification itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the Glossary for definitions frequently used in the Guide and in the Classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope Interpretation within Hierarchically Superior Places
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of any classification place must always be interpreted within the scope of all its hierarchically superior places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining scope read group/subgroup/main group within the context of subclass, class, subsection, section titles, references, and notes which may restrict or modify interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles Generally Broad; Subclass/Main Group/Subgroup Titles More Precise
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of sections and subsections are broadly indicative and do not precisely define subject matter; subclass titles (with references/definitions/notes) aim to define scope as precisely as possible; main group and subgroup titles (subject to references/notes) precisely define the subject matter covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on broad section/subsection titles; read subclass/main group/subgroup titles together with their references, definitions, and notes for precise scope (examples and illustrations provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Places Can Cover More Than Explicitly Stated Scope (68bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain circumstances, a place can cover more than its explicitly stated scope: (a) details/components specially adapted for or used only with the explicitly stated subject matter and not provided elsewhere; (b) combinations of the explicitly stated subject matter with other subject matter; (c) subject matter of a category not covered by the place and not covered elsewhere but related to the explicitly stated subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and cross-references are provided (see paragraphs 92–98 for related guidance). Use this rule cautiously and in context with references and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Subclasses
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a subclass is defined collectively by: (a) the subclass title, (b) any limiting references following the subclass/class title, (c) any limiting references which appear in groups of the subclass referring subject matter elsewhere, and (d) any notes under the subclass title or its class/subsection/section title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting references may exclude substantial parts of a field; notes can define terms or clarify relations between places. The subclass should include all subject matter specifically stated in its main group titles even if not apparent from the subclass title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Main Groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a main group is to be interpreted within the scope of its subclass and is determined by the main group title as modified by relevant references or notes associated with the main group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A main group for a topic in a subclass limited to a particular apparatus covers only features peculiar to that apparatus. Definitions may provide more detail. Guidance headings are informative only and usually do not define or modify scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Subgroups and Indentation Reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a subgroup is interpreted within its subclass, main group, and any higher indented subgroup titles; subgroup scope is determined by its title as modified by associated references or notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read indented subgroup titles as qualifying the scope of the higher-level group (examples given for A63B). A subgroup covers only a portion of the subject matter of the parent group, devised to serve as a self-contained field of search; essential characteristics in subgroup titles determine scope (cases where essential characteristics are or are not expressed in parent title).

rubrics_metrics.name: File Scope of Groups
rubrics_metrics.description: File scope is the subject matter that should actually be classified in a group itself (i.e., the residual subject matter not covered by its subgroups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a group has no subgroups, scope and file scope are identical. When new subgroups are created, group scope remains unchanged but file scope is reduced. Treat file scope as residual matter for classification into the parent group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary Purpose: Facilitate Retrieval; Single Place for Same Technical Subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of the Classification is to facilitate retrieval; therefore the system is devised and must be used so that one and the same technical subject is classified in, and can be retrieved from, one and the same place — the place most relevant to searches for that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing classification, prefer the single most relevant place to improve retrievability; apply consistent judgment across documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention Information Definition and Determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention information is technical information in the total disclosure of a patent document that represents an addition to the state of the art; it is determined in the context of the state of the art using guidance provided by the claims with due regard to the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The meaning of 'addition to the state of the art' is novel and unobvious subject matter specifically disclosed and not part of prior art; selection rules for classification symbols are the same for invention and additional information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Information Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional information is non-trivial technical information which does not in itself represent an addition to the state of the art but might constitute useful information for the searcher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It complements invention information by identifying constituents, elements/components, or uses/applications that aid searching; classification selection rules apply equally to additional information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical subject matter may represent processes, products, apparatus or materials (or the way these are used or applied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret these categories broadly; examples are provided (e.g., polymerisation = process; chemical compounds = products; installations = apparatus; ingredients = materials). Apparatus can be regarded as a product, but 'product' often denotes the result of a process while 'apparatus' denotes intended use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifying a Technical Subject as a Whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classification is designed to ensure that any technical subject with which an invention is essentially concerned can be classified, as far as possible, as a whole and not by separate classification of constituent parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, constituent parts may also constitute invention information if they themselves are novel and unobvious, in which case classification of both the whole and the parts is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-oriented, Application-oriented and Residual Places
rubrics_metrics.description: Places exist for: (a) a thing 'in general' (function-oriented), (b) a thing 'specially adapted for' a particular use (application-oriented), (c) the particular use or application, and (d) the incorporation of a thing into a larger system; residual places are to be considered only if no other place provides for the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate each category (e.g., F16K valves = function-oriented; A61F 2/24 mechanical valve for insertion into a human heart = specially adapted). Words like 'not otherwise provided for' designate residual places. A given place may be more or less function- or application-oriented relative to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to Use Function-oriented vs Application-oriented Places
rubrics_metrics.description: If a particular application is mentioned but not specifically disclosed or fully identified, classify in the function-oriented place if available. If essential technical characteristics relate both to intrinsic nature and to a particular use/special adaptation/incorporation, classify in both function-oriented and application-oriented places. If none of these guide the decision, classify in both function-oriented and relevant application-oriented places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the three-part test (paragraph 90): (a) unclear application -> function-oriented; (b) essential characteristics both intrinsic and use-related -> both; (c) otherwise -> both. Use available Definitions and references to decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifying Larger Systems and Their Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: When classifying a larger system as a whole, attention should be given to parts or details whenever they are novel and unobvious; classification of both the system and these parts/details is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: classify a vehicle suspension system in B60G, and if a leaf spring itself is novel/unobvious classify also in F16F. Consider both system-level and component-level invention information.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a Category Is Not Explicitly Provided for in Titles
rubrics_metrics.description: If the technical subject may be expressed as different categories (process/product/apparatus/material) and no distinct place exists for one category, use the most appropriate place existing for the other categories; Definitions and references may indicate appropriate places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See detailed rules for chemical matter and other special situations (paragraphs 93–99). Use references, notes, definitions, or similar subject matter provision in other groups to determine placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic Table Default
rubrics_metrics.description: In all sections of the IPC, in the absence of an indication to the contrary, the Periodic Table with eighteen groups (Arabic numerals) is the one referred to; where the contrary is indicated, the system with eight groups (Roman numerals) may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check specific group indications; example groups cited (D06M 11/13 vs H01F 1/00).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Chemical Compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject concerns a chemical compound per se, it is classified in section C according to its chemical structure. When it also concerns a specific field of use, it is also classified in the place for that field if the field of use is an essential technical characteristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the compound is known and the invention concerns only its application, classify in the field-of-use place as invention information, while the chemical structure may be classified in the compound place as additional information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Chemical Mixtures or Compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject concerns a chemical mixture/composition per se, classify in a place according to its chemical composition if such a place exists; if not, classify according to its use or application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the use/application is an essential technical characteristic, classify according to both composition and use. If the mixture/composition is known and only its use is the invention information, classify in field-of-use place for invention information and composition place as additional information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Preparation or Treatment of Compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject concerns a process of preparation or treatment of a chemical compound, classify in the place for the process of preparation/treatment of that compound. If such a place does not exist, classify in the place for the compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the compound resulting from the process is novel, also classify the compound according to its chemical structure. General processes for classes of compounds are classified in groups for the processes used when such groups exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Apparatus or Processes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject concerns an apparatus, classify in the place for the apparatus if such a place exists; if not, classify the apparatus in the place for the process performed by that apparatus. If the subject concerns a process for making/treating products, classify in the place for the process; if none exists, classify in the place for the apparatus performing the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no place exists for the manufacture of a product, classify the manufacturing apparatus/process in the place covering the product. Use available group titles, references, and definitions to decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Articles of Manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject concerns an article, classify in the place for the article. If no place exists for the article itself, classify in the appropriate function-oriented place (by function) or, if that is not possible, according to the field of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: glue-dispenser specially adapted for binding books is classified in B42C 9/00 (applying glue peculiar to bookbinding) because no specific place for glue-dispensers for bookbinding exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Multistep Processes and Industrial Plants
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject concerns a multistep process or an industrial plant consisting of combinations of process steps or apparatus, classify as a whole in a place provided for such combinations; if no such place exists, classify in the place for the product obtained by the process or plant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subject also concerns an element of the combination (e.g., an individual step or machine), classify the element separately as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Details and Constructional Parts (Rules a–d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for details/parts: (a) details/parts only applicable to or specially adapted for one kind of subject matter are classified in the details places of that kind if such places exist; (b) if such places do not exist, classify in the place for the subject matter; (c) details/parts applicable to more than one kind of subject matter are classified in more general details places if such exist; (d) if such general places do not exist, classify according to all kinds of subject matter to which they explicitly apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate classifications (e.g., subclass A45B details vs kinds of umbrellas). Apply the rule hierarchy (a→b→c→d) depending on availability of detail-places and applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Chemical Formulae Classification Procedure — Step 1 (Fully Identified Compounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: When chemical compounds are specified using a general formula (large genus or Markush-type claims), classification should be given to all 'fully identified' compounds that are novel and unobvious if they are (i) specifically claimed as such or in a composition, (ii) products of a claimed process, or (iii) derivatives of either of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A compound is 'fully identified' where: (a) the structure is given by exact chemical name or formula, or can be deduced from its preparation from specified reactants with at most one selected from a list of alternatives; and (b) the compound is characterised by a physical property (e.g., melting point), or its preparation is described in a worked example giving practical details. Compounds identified only by an empirical formula are not 'fully identified'. (Further steps continue beyond Step 1 in subsequent guidance.)
